title: Watercolour wet-on-wet: let the water do the painting
description: The most magical watercolour technique needs the least control: wet the paper first, then drop in colour and watch it bloom. Why the paint spreads, and how to steer a technique that refuses to be steered.

body.heading: Wet paper changes everything
paragraphs: Brush clean water over your paper until it shines, then touch in a loaded brush of colour. Instead of staying where you put it, the pigment travels — drifting, feathering and mingling with whatever colour it meets. The paint is not being disobedient; it is simply moving through the water film, the way ink spreads through a wet tissue.

That bloom is exactly why wet-on-wet is the classic way to paint skies, water, distant hills and soft shadows: the subjects that have no hard edges in real life should not have hard edges on paper either.

body.heading: Steering without forcing
paragraphs: You cannot command wet-on-wet, but you can nudge it. Tilt the board and gravity walks the colour downhill. Use less water for a shorter, moodier spread; more water for a pale wash that travels far. Drop a second colour beside the first while both are wet and they will marry in the middle with a blend no brush could mix.

Work fast and forgive quickly — the window lasts only while the paper keeps its shine. Once it turns dull, the same stroke sits still and behaves, and you have accidentally invented the second technique: wet-on-dry, for edges and details.

body.heading: A first painting that cannot fail
paragraphs: Try a sunset strip: wet the whole page, then bands of yellow, orange and pink from top to bottom, letting each bleed into the next. While it dries — untouched, however tempted you are — the sky paints itself. When it is bone dry, add a black silhouette of rooftops or a tree in wet-on-dry on top.
Two techniques, one picture, and the oldest lesson in watercolour: the water is not your servant or your enemy. It is your co-painter.

takeaway: Wet the paper, drop in colour and let it bloom: wet-on-wet paints skies and water beautifully precisely because you give up control.
